The finding

Other model families can grade a logic translation without a gold formula

Can we tell whether a first-order logic (FOL) translation says what its sentence says when no gold formula exists?

Gold references are expensive and often wrong: a recent audit of two standard benchmarks found errors in 39 to 42% of their annotations. The paper studies a gold-free alternative. Several independent LLM families translate the same sentence, the solver checks which translations are logically equivalent, and each candidate gets a : the fraction of whose translation is not equivalent to it.

When translators share a supplied predicate vocabulary (), consensus reaches a of 0.954 on 221 fresh long-exception sentences with trusted references and pure Z3 labels. A API judge reaches 0.587 on the same items.

+0.367

AUROC gained over the disguised flash-lite judge on shared-signature sentences, 95% sentence-cluster bootstrap CI [+0.328, +0.404].

Under , consensus still beats the judges (+0.099 on the development set, +0.171 on untouched sentences against the original-view judge), but the gain shrinks by roughly 0.15 AUROC, and the that free vocabulary needs raises false alarms on meaning-preserving renames. Confirmation on independent held-out data was budget-stopped and remains incomplete.

    If only some model families were available, or you wanted fewer false alarms, what would consensus look like?

      The name-free ignores predicate names. Development set E, PERTURB suite: meaning-preserving renames of CORRECT base formulas. is the false-alarm rate the rename alone adds (FA minus base FA). Recall is at the primary threshold on typed mutants.

      What the paper does not show

      • No completed confirmation. A fresh held-out set (E2-A, 550 new sentences) was built, but the run's budget ran out before enough items were labelled. On its one testable stratum (DT, short ProverQA sentences) consensus reaches a stratified AUROC of 0.916 and ties a local Qwen-8B judge (Δ = +0.003 [−0.042, +0.052]). On L25 sentences it falls to 0.443 on only 42 items (35 ERROR / 7 CORRECT from 3 sentences), an estimate with extreme variance. Every pre-registered criterion on the target strata returned NOT_TESTABLE or unfavourable.
      • Shared-signature scope. The 0.954 result uses templated sentences with a supplied predicate vocabulary, which removes the alignment problem. It does not extend to translators who choose their own predicate names.
      • Development data overlap. R_COMP-SIG later served as development data for aligner tuning, so the development-set numbers from E are not independent of it.
      • Rename vulnerability. Under free vocabulary, a 76.5% false-alarm rate on nonce renames means the metric penalises translations with non-standard predicate names even when they are correct.
      • Length degradation. Under free vocabulary, discrimination degrades with sentence length (NET +0.356), driven by correct translations that diverge. The metric is weakest on the long, heavily conditioned sentences where gold-free evaluation matters most.
      • Provisional labels. R_COMP FREE uses because the gloss gate failed twice (balanced accuracy 0.776, then 0.561, against a 0.90 bar). On the two-auditor subset the gain over the original-view judge is +0.105 [+0.011, +0.215], a CI that barely excludes zero.
      • Label dependence and domain. Labels on E come from a panel whose agreement is imperfect. All results are English to FOL from MALLS, ProverQA and R_COMP; other formalisms, languages and sentence distributions are untested.
      • Cost. At k = 9, consensus costs $0.91 per 10,000 candidates (amortised); a single cheap judge call costs $0.51 per 10,000.
